items.title: The CBD paragraph, in your words
items.your_version:
I would also use topical magnesium chloride and consider topical DMSO with a known-genuine CBD preparation as adjuncts (a lot of CBD is fake or very dilute). Seizures come in all different types, and we have no study on whether CBD could be a rescue remedy for a seizure ([just anecdotes](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RCxGSrUsB0Q)), even though we do have studies showing long-term effectiveness to prevent them: Purified oral CBD is approved for the seizures of Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, Dravet syndrome and tuberous sclerosis complex. For focal seizures outside those syndromes, the evidence is mixed, but still long-term. 

And topical CBD hasn't been well-studied. There was a short 12-week trial done, where they used a CBD skin gel, and it did show that transdermal absorption works like oral CBD's but the dosing was too low, and transdermal CBD also doesn't get converted to the potentially more active form (7-OH-CBD) by the liver. 

As for DMSO, it did reduce seizure activity in a rats with temporal-lobe epilepsy, and we know it has several neuroprotective mechanisms, but it produced the opposite effect at some doses in an absence-epilepsy model. I'd treat it as a plausible experimental adjunct remedy rather than something to wait on while a seizure continues.

items.my_version: I would also use topical magnesium chloride and consider topical DMSO with a known CBD preparation as adjuncts. Purified oral CBD is approved for the seizures of Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, Dravet syndrome and tuberous sclerosis complex. For focal seizures outside those syndromes, the evidence is mixed. In a 12-week trial, a CBD skin gel reached the blood at levels like oral CBD's but did no better than placebo. In a 2025 study of high-dose oral CBD, around 23 mg/kg a day (about 1,400 mg for a 60 kg adult), focal seizures fell by about half to three quarters over nearly three years, but it had no placebo group to compare with. None of it tested CBD as rapid seizure rescue. DMSO reduced seizure activity in a rat temporal-lobe epilepsy model and has several neuroprotective mechanisms, but it produced the opposite effect at some doses in an absence-epilepsy model. I treat it as a plausible experimental adjunct rather than something to wait on while a seizure continues.

items.title: The first five minutes: the dangers paragraph, in your words
items.where: Psychological First Aid: The First Five Minutes, P3
items.your_version: Anything that could let someone hurt themselves in the next five minutes take priority, so get the car keys out of reach and turn the stove off, and move them away from roads and balconies, or pools of water for that matter. Put any weapons away and keep the person away from crowds and strangers. If they want to post their big revelation about the universe, or message an ex, take the phone.
